lessons.title: los meses — the calendar's gods and Caesars
lessons.gloss: the months — Roman gods and emperors, marching almost unchanged from Latin

segments.text: Spanish's twelve months are a procession of Roman gods and emperors, barely changed from Latin. Two things you already know pay off immediately: marzo is the war-god you met in martes, and septiembre–diciembre are the Latin numbers 7–10 from the counting chapters.

utterances: Spanish: enero. from Latin: Iānuārius. who / what: Janus, the two-faced god of doors & beginnings.
Spanish: febrero. from Latin: Februārius. who / what: Februa, the Roman purification festival.
Spanish: marzo. from Latin: Martius. who / what: Mars, the war-god — the same Mars as martes (Tuesday)!
Spanish: abril. from Latin: Aprīlis. who / what: perhaps aperīre, "to open" (buds opening).
Spanish: mayo. from Latin: Māius. who / what: Maia, goddess of growth.
Spanish: junio. from Latin: Iūnius. who / what: Juno, queen of the gods.
Spanish: julio. from Latin: Iūlius. who / what: originally Quīntīlis, "the 5th [month]" — renamed for Julius Caesar after his death.
Spanish: agosto. from Latin: Augustus. who / what: originally Sextīlis, "the 6th [month]" — renamed for the emperor Augustus.
Spanish: septiembre. from Latin: september. who / what: "7th" (septem).
Spanish: octubre. from Latin: octōber. who / what: "8th" (octō).
Spanish: noviembre. from Latin: november. who / what: "9th" (novem).
Spanish: diciembre. from Latin: december. who / what: "10th" (decem).

segments.text: marzo = Mars = martes. The month and the weekday honor the same war-god — Martius (his month) and Martis diēs (his day). Spot one, you know the other.

The 7–10 months. Septiembre through diciembre still carry septem, octō, novem, decem — because the old Roman year originally began in March, with September genuinely the 7th month. Centuries before Caesar, two new months (Januarius, Februarius) were added at the front to cover the winter, which pushed every later month's number out of step with its name — September became the 9th month while still being named "7th." Julius and Augustus had nothing to do with that shift: they simply got two already-existing months — Quintilis and Sextilis, literally "5th" and "6th" — renamed in their honor after the fact. The names stuck; the months themselves were never new.

segments.instruction: the tie-back — "marzo / martes — both Mars, the war-god"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the tie-back — "marzo / martes — both Mars, the war-god"]
[YOU SAY: "septiembre = 7, diciembre = 10" — the old March-start year]

segments.text: Which god links marzo and martes? (Mars, the war-god — his month and his day.) Why is diciembre Latin for "ten"? (The Roman year began in March, and adding January/February at the front later pushed every month's number out of step with its name.) Did Julius Caesar and Augustus add new months to the calendar? (No — julio and agosto were already-existing months, Quintilis and Sextilis ("5th"/"6th"), simply renamed in their honor.)
